{{Short description|Number theory theorem}}
{{For|the theorem in complex analysis|Gauss–Lucas theorem}}
In [[number theory]], '''Lucas's theorem''' expresses the [[remainder]] of division of the [[binomial coefficient]] <math>\tbinom{m}{n}</math> by a [[prime number]] ''p'' in terms of the [[radix|base]] ''p'' expansions of the integers ''m'' and ''n''.

Lucas's theorem first appeared in 1878 in papers by [[Édouard Lucas]].<ref>
*{{cite journal| author=Edouard Lucas |title=Théorie des Fonctions Numériques Simplement Périodiques| jstor=2369308 |journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics]] |year=1878 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=184–196 |doi=10.2307/2369308| mr=1505161}} (part 1);
*{{cite journal| author=Edouard Lucas |title=Théorie des Fonctions Numériques Simplement Périodiques| jstor=2369311 |journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics]] |year=1878 |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=197–240 |doi=10.2307/2369311| mr=1505164}} (part 2);
*{{cite journal| author=Edouard Lucas |title=Théorie des Fonctions Numériques Simplement Périodiques| jstor=2369373 |journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics]] |year=1878 |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=289–321 |doi=10.2307/2369373| mr=1505176}} (part 3)</ref>

== Statement ==
For non-negative integers ''m'' and ''n'' and a prime ''p'', the following [[modular arithmetic|congruence relation]] holds:
:<math>\binom{m}{n}\equiv\prod_{i=0}^k\binom{m_i}{n_i}\pmod p,</math>
where
:<math>m=m_kp^k+m_{k-1}p^{k-1}+\cdots +m_1p+m_0,</math>
and
:<math>n=n_kp^k+n_{k-1}p^{k-1}+\cdots +n_1p+n_0</math>
are the [[Positional notation|base ''p'' expansions]] of ''m'' and ''n'' respectively.  This uses the convention that <math>\tbinom{m}{n} = 0</math> if ''m''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''n''.

== Proofs ==

There are several ways to prove Lucas's theorem. 

{{Math proof|title=Combinatorial proof using a group action|drop=hidden|proof=
Let ''M'' be a set with ''m'' elements, and arbitrarily divide it into ''m<sub>i</sub>'' cycles of length ''p<sup>i</sup>'' for the various values of ''i''.  Then each of these cycles can be rotated separately by a [[cyclic group]] ''C<sub>p<sup>i</sup></sub>'', so that the [[group (mathematics)|group]] ''G'' which is the [[direct product of groups|Cartesian product]] of all these cyclic groups (one for each cycle) [[group action|acts on]] ''M''.  It thus also acts on the set of ''n''-element subsets ''N'' of ''M'', the number of which is <math>\tbinom{m}{n}</math>. This is the group action we consider in the sequel.  

Since the number of elements in ''G'' is a power of ''p'', the same is true of any of its [[Group action#Orbits and stabilizers|orbits]], by the [[Group_action#Orbit–stabilizer_theorem|orbit-stabilizer theorem]].  Hence, <math>\tbinom{m}{n}</math> is congruent modulo ''p'' to the number of sets ''N'' whose orbit is of size 1, i.e., to the number of [[fixed_point_(mathematics)#Fixed_point_of_a_group_action|fixed points]] of the group action.  

Since all cycles can be independently rotated by our group ''G'', the fixed points of the action are those subsets ''N'' that are a union of some of the cycles.  This means that ''N'' must consist of exactly ''n<sub>i</sub>'' cycles of size ''p<sup>i</sup>'' for each ''i'', for the same reason that the integer ''n'' has a unique representation in base ''p''.  Thus the number of choices for ''N'' is exactly
<math>\prod_{i=0}^k\binom{m_i}{n_i}</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof based on generating functions|drop=hidden|proof=
This proof is due to [[Nathan Fine]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Fine|first=Nathan|author-link=Nathan Fine|title=Binomial coefficients modulo a prime|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|year=1947|volume=54|issue=10|pages=589–592|doi=10.2307/2304500|jstor=2304500}}</ref>

If ''p'' is a prime and ''n'' is an integer with 1 ≤ ''n'' ≤ ''p'' − 1, then the numerator of the binomial coefficient
:<math> \binom p n = \frac{p \cdot (p-1) \cdots (p-n+1)}{n \cdot (n-1) \cdots 1} </math>
is divisible by ''p'' but the denominator is not.  Hence ''p'' divides <math>\tbinom{p}{n}</math>.  Because of the [[binomial theorem]], this means that
:<math>(1+X)^p\equiv1+X^p\pmod{p}.</math>
Continuing by [[mathematical induction|induction]], we have for every nonnegative integer ''i'' that
:<math>(1+X)^{p^i}\equiv1+X^{p^i}\pmod{p}.</math>

Now let ''m'' be a nonnegative integer, and let ''p'' be a prime.  Write ''m'' in base ''p'', so that <math>m=\sum_{i=0}^{k}m_ip^i</math> for some nonnegative integer ''k'' and integers ''m''<sub>''i''</sub> with 0 ≤ ''m''<sub>''i''</sub> ≤ ''p'' − 1.  Then
:<math>\begin{align}
\sum_{n=0}^{m}\binom{m}{n}X^n &
=(1+X)^m=\prod_{i=0}^{k}\left((1+X)^{p^i}\right)^{m_i}\\
 & \equiv \prod_{i=0}^{k}\left(1+X^{p^i}\right)^{m_i}\\
&=\prod_{i=0}^{k}\left(\sum_{j_i=0}^{m_i}\binom{m_i}{j_i}X^{j_ip^i}\right)\\
 & =\sum_{n=0}^{m}\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k}\binom{m_i}{n_i}\right)X^n
\pmod{p}.
\end{align}</math>
In the last equality we use [[distributive property|distributivity]] and the fact that the representation of ''n'' in base ''p'' is unique, where ''n''<sub>''i''</sub> is the ''i''-th digit in the base ''p'' representation of ''n''.  Comparing the coefficients of ''X''<sup>''n''</sup> in the very first and last sum, we obtain Lucas's theorem.
}}
[[File:Sierpinski Pascal triangle.svg|thumb|Pascal's triangle, showing the odd binomial coefficients in black.]]

== Consequences ==
One consequence of Lucas's theorem is that the binomial coefficient <math>\tbinom{m}{n}</math> is divisible by the prime ''p'' [[if and only if]] at least one of the digits of the base-''p'' representation of ''n'' is greater than the corresponding digit of ''m''.  In particular, <math>\tbinom{m}{n}</math> is [[Parity (mathematics)|odd]] if and only if the positions of the ones in the [[binary expansion]] of ''n'' are a subset of the positions of the ones in that of ''m''. This leads to a peculiar distribution of odd numbers in [[Pascal's triangle]], resembling [[Sierpiński triangle|Sierpiński 's triangle]], shown to the right.

== Non-prime moduli ==

Lucas's theorem can be generalized to give an expression for the remainder when <math>\tbinom mn</math> is divided by a [[prime power]] ''p''<sup>''k''</sup>. However, the formulas become more complicated.

If the modulus is the square of a prime ''p'', the following congruence relation holds for all 0 ≤ ''s'' ≤ ''r'' ≤ ''p'' − 1, ''a'' ≥ 0, and ''b'' ≥ 0:
:<math>\binom{pa+r}{pb+s}\equiv\binom ab\binom rs(1+pa(H_r-H_{r-s})+pb(H_{r-s}-H_s))\pmod{p^2},</math>
where <math>H_n=1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\cdots+\tfrac1n</math> is the ''n''th [[harmonic number]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Rowland |first=Eric |title=Lucas' theorem modulo ''p''<sup>2</sup> |doi=10.1080/00029890.2022.2038004 |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |volume=129 |year=2022 |issue=9 |pages=846–855 |arxiv=2006.11701v3}}</ref>  Generalizations of Lucas's theorem for higher prime powers ''p''<sup>''k''</sup> are also given by Davis and Webb (1990)<ref>{{cite journal |author=Kenneth S. Davis, William A. Webb |title=Lucas' Theorem for Prime Powers |journal=European Journal of Combinatorics |volume=11 |issue=3 |year=1990 |pages=229–233 |doi=10.1016/S0195-6698(13)80122-9|doi-access= }}</ref> and Granville (1997).<ref>{{cite journal |author=[[Andrew Granville]] |title=Arithmetic Properties of Binomial Coefficients I: Binomial coefficients modulo prime powers |journal=Canadian Mathematical Society Conference Proceedings |volume=20 |pages=253–275 |year=1997 |url=http://www.dms.umontreal.ca/%7Eandrew/PDF/BinCoeff.pdf |mr=1483922 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202003812/http://www.dms.umontreal.ca/~andrew/PDF/BinCoeff.pdf |archivedate=2017-02-02 }}</ref>

[[Kummer's theorem]] asserts that the largest [[integer]] ''k'' such that ''p''<sup>''k''</sup> divides the binomial coefficient <math>\tbinom{m}{n}</math> (or in other words, the [[p-adic valuation|valuation]] of the binomial coefficient  with respect to the prime ''p'') is equal to the number of [[Carry (arithmetic)|carries]] that occur when ''n'' and ''m''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''n'' are added in the [[Positional notation#Base of the numeral system|base ''p'']].

== ''q''-binomial coefficients ==

There is a generalization of Lucas's theorem for the [[q-binomial coefficient|''q''-binomial coefficients]].  It asserts that if ''a'', ''b'', ''r'', ''s'', ''k'' are integers, where 0 ≤ ''b'', ''s'' < ''k'', then
<math display=block> \begin{bmatrix} ka+b \\ kr+s \end{bmatrix}_q \equiv \binom{a}{r} \begin{bmatrix} b \\ s  \end{bmatrix}_q \mod{\Phi_k},</math> where {{tmath|\begin{bmatrix} ka+b \\ kr+s \end{bmatrix}_q}} and {{tmath|\begin{bmatrix} b \\ s \end{bmatrix}_q}} are ''q''-binomial coefficients, <math>\binom{a}{r}</math> is a usual binomial coefficient, and {{tmath|\Phi_k}} is the ''k''th [[cyclotomic polynomial]] (in the variable ''q'').<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Désarménien |first1=Jacques |title=Un Analogue des Congruences de Kummer pour les q-nombres d'Euler |journal=European Journal of Combinatorics |date=March 1982 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=19–28 |doi=10.1016/S0195-6698(82)80005-X|doi-access= }}</ref>
